title: How To Give A Consequence That Really Works
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin treats the physical delivery of a consequence as a learnable, repeatable performance, not just a policy decision, comparing it to the choreographed steps of a tango. He lays out an eight-step sequence: wait a beat and observe the misbehavior fully before moving, scan to ensure it doesn't spread to other students, decide which rule was broken, make eye contact (moving closer only if needed), state the consequence plainly and briefly ('You have a warning because you broke rule number two'), then turn away immediately before the student can argue, and monitor compliance afterward without staring directly at the student. His emphasis throughout is on dispassionate, detached delivery -- comparing the teacher's demeanor to a referee calling a play -- because emotional or hesitant delivery undermines the message and invites negotiation. He recommends literally practicing the sequence, including in front of a mirror or with a colleague's feedback, treating consistency of timing and temperament as a distinct, masterable skill separate from simply having the right consequences in place.

State the consequence in a fixed, brief script (e.g., 'You have a warning because you broke rule number two') rather than explaining or elaborating.
Turn away immediately after stating the consequence, before the student can argue or protest, to avoid turning it into a negotiation.

quotes: How you give a consequence matters. It’s not just do or not do. The way it’s performed goes a long way toward your students taking responsibility.
The latter requires a distinct pathway, or steps of a great dance, like the rhythmic turns and whirls of an Argentine tango.
Widen your field of vision to ensure others are not or will not get involved. Don’t move an inch forward until you’ve taken a full account of the transgression. Rushing in is a common mistake.
Stop as soon as you make eye contact, direct all four fingers of your hand toward them, and say “You have a warning because you broke rule number two.” (For example)
Pause a beat while maintaining eye contact, then turn away abruptly before the student can protest, argue , or excuse their behavior. Immediately, go back to what you were doing.
You must be absolutely consistent in your follow through and temperament. It’s an underappreciated and oft-overlooked key to classroom management success.
Practice in your empty classroom if you need to. Do it in front of a mirror. Have a colleague watch you and provide feedback.
